questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 2(42) · Definition of foreign company
questions.stem: Under section 2(42) of the Companies Act 2013, a 'foreign company' means any company or body corporate incorporated outside India which:

readLink.label: Read: The definition of a foreign company — s. 2(42) →

options.text: Sells goods or provides services to customers situated in India, in whatever manner
options.explanation: Doing business WITH India is not the test. A German manufacturer that ships goods against orders placed from Germany, with no office, agent or electronic presence here, has no place of business in India and is not a foreign company.

options.text: Has a place of business in India, whether by itself or through an agent, physically or through electronic mode, AND conducts any business activity in India in any other manner
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(42) has three limbs and they are cumulative — incorporation outside India, a place of business in India (by itself or through an agent, physically or through electronic mode), and the conduct of business activity in India.

options.text: Has a place of business in India, whether or not it conducts any business activity here
options.explanation: This drops the third limb. A flat leased in Mumbai purely as a guest house for visiting staff is a presence without business activity, and the definition is not satisfied.

options.text: Has at least one shareholder or director who is resident in India
options.explanation: Residence of shareholders or directors is irrelevant to s. 2(42). Indian shareholding matters only for the separate 50% test in s. 379(2), which presupposes that the company is already a foreign company.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 2(42) · Place of business through an agent
questions.stem: Regarding the 'place of business in India' limb of section 2(42), which statement is correct?

readLink.label: Read: The definition of a foreign company — s. 2(42) →

options.text: The place of business must be owned or leased by the company itself; an agent's premises are never enough
options.explanation: The sub-clause says 'whether by itself or through an agent'. A standing establishment maintained by the company's agent in India satisfies the limb.

options.text: The place of business must be a physical location; a purely electronic presence cannot satisfy the limb
options.explanation: The sub-clause expressly says 'physically or through electronic mode', and Rule 2(1)(c) of the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules 2014 defines electronic mode very widely.

options.text: The place of business may be maintained by the company itself or through an agent, and may be physical or through electronic mode
options.explanation: Correct. Section 2(42)(a) covers all four permutations — by itself or through an agent, physically or through electronic mode. Only one of them need be present.

options.text: A share transfer or registration office is expressly excluded from the expression 'place of business'
options.explanation: The opposite is true. Section 386(c) provides that 'place of business' INCLUDES a share transfer or registration office.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · Rule 2(1)(c) · Electronic mode
questions.stem: Kestrel Analytics Inc, incorporated in the United States, runs a subscription analytics platform used by 4,000 Indian businesses. Its main server is located in Virginia and it has no premises in India. For the purpose of the 'electronic mode' limb of section 2(42):
questions.sourceRef: Rule 2(1)(c), Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: The definition of a foreign company — s. 2(42) →

options.text: The location of the main server is irrelevant — electronic mode is defined to apply whether or not the main server is installed in India
options.explanation: Correct. Rule 2(1)(c) defines electronic mode as carrying out transactions electronically 'whether the main server is installed in India or not', and expressly names business-to-business and business-to-consumer transactions and online services.

options.text: Electronic mode is satisfied only if the main server is installed in India
options.explanation: That is exactly what the Rule negatives. A server-location test would defeat the purpose of the electronic-mode limb, which was inserted to reach companies with no physical presence here.

options.text: Electronic mode covers only the acceptance of deposits and subscriptions in securities from Indian citizens
options.explanation: That is one head in a long list. The Rule also covers business-to-business and business-to-consumer transactions, data interchange, financial settlements, web-based marketing, advisory and transactional services, database services, supply-chain management and online services.

options.text: Electronic mode is defined in section 2(42) itself, and the Rules add nothing
options.explanation: Section 2(42) uses the phrase but does not define it. The definition sits in Rule 2(1)(c) of the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules 2014 — which is why it is rules-level and amendment-sensitive.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 386(c) · Place of business
questions.stem: For the purposes of Chapter XXII, section 386 provides that the expression 'place of business':

readLink.label: Read: Interpretation — s. 386 →

options.text: Means only premises owned by the company in India
options.explanation: Section 386(c) is an inclusive provision, not a restrictive one, and ownership of the premises is nowhere made the test.

options.text: Excludes any office that does not generate revenue
options.explanation: No such exclusion exists. Whether business activity is conducted is a separate limb of s. 2(42); revenue generation at the particular office is not the statutory test.

options.text: Means the principal place of business notified to the Registrar under section 380(1)(e)
options.explanation: Section 380(1)(e) requires the principal place of business to be notified, but that does not narrow the meaning of 'place of business' — a company may have many, and s. 381(4) requires a list of them all.

options.text: Includes a share transfer or registration office
options.explanation: Correct. Section 386(c) provides that 'place of business' includes a share transfer or registration office, so a foreign company maintaining nothing here but a registrar-and-transfer office has a place of business in India.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 2(42) · Isolated transactions
questions.stem: Nordwind GmbH, incorporated in Germany, concludes one export sale to an Indian buyer by e-mail and appoints no representative here. On the question whether it has established a place of business in India:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 2(42); ICAI SM P2 Ch 11 analysis

readLink.label: Read: The definition of a foreign company — s. 2(42) →

options.text: It has, because the contract was concluded with a person in India
options.explanation: Concluding a contract with an Indian counterparty is business WITH India, not a place of business IN India. Otherwise every overseas exporter would be a foreign company.

options.text: It has not — an isolated transaction does not by itself amount to establishing a place of business
options.explanation: Correct. The definition contemplates a settled, continuing presence from which business is done. A single transaction, without any office, agent or standing electronic establishment, does not establish a place of business.

options.text: It has, because e-mail correspondence is 'electronic mode' under the Rules
options.explanation: Electronic mode contemplates carrying on business electronically through a continuing establishment or platform. Using e-mail to negotiate one sale is a means of communication, not the maintenance of a place of business.

options.text: The question cannot arise unless the company is already registered with the Registrar
options.explanation: Registration is the consequence of being a foreign company, not the condition of becoming one. The definition is applied first; the s. 380 filing follows.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 379(2) · Fifty per cent aggregation
questions.stem: Aurelia Systems Inc, incorporated in Delaware and having a branch office in Hyderabad, has paid-up capital of ₹40,00,000 of equity and ₹10,00,000 of preference. The equity is held as to ₹12,00,000 by Indian citizens, ₹9,00,000 by Sundar Infotech Private Limited (incorporated in India) and ₹19,00,000 by its Delaware parent. The preference is held as to ₹4,00,000 by Sundar Infotech Private Limited and ₹6,00,000 by a Cayman fund. The percentage of the paid-up share capital held by Indian citizens and Indian-incorporated bodies corporate is:

readLink.label: Read: Indian-held foreign companies — s. 379 →

options.explanation: That counts only the Indian citizens' ₹12,00,000 against the total of ₹50,00,000 and ignores the Indian company's holding, which section 379(2) expressly aggregates.

That counts the Indian holders' equity of ₹21,00,000 against the total paid-up capital of ₹50,00,000, dropping the ₹4,00,000 of preference from the numerator while keeping preference in the denominator.

Correct. Total paid-up share capital is ₹50,00,000; the qualifying holding is ₹12,00,000 (Indian citizens) plus ₹9,00,000 and ₹4,00,000 (an Indian-incorporated company) = ₹25,00,000, which is 50%. Since section 379(2) says 'not less than fifty per cent', the test is satisfied.

That is ₹21,00,000 of equity against ₹40,00,000 of equity — the right answer to the wrong question. Section 379(2) covers capital 'whether equity or preference or partly equity and partly preference', so both classes go into the numerator AND the denominator.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 379(2) · Who counts in the 50%
questions.stem: Belvoir Trading Ltd, incorporated in the United Kingdom and having a liaison office in Kolkata, has paid-up share capital of ₹80,00,000. Of this, ₹18,00,000 is held by citizens of India, ₹20,00,000 by companies incorporated in India, ₹6,00,000 by persons of Indian origin who hold foreign passports and are not citizens of India, and ₹36,00,000 by the UK parent. The percentage relevant to the section 379(2) test is:

readLink.label: Read: Indian-held foreign companies — s. 379 →

options.explanation: That is the Indian citizens' ₹18,00,000 alone. Section 379(2) aggregates citizens of India AND companies or bodies corporate incorporated in India, singly or in the aggregate.

Correct. Only citizens of India (₹18,00,000) and Indian-incorporated bodies corporate (₹20,00,000) qualify — ₹38,00,000 of ₹80,00,000 = 47.5%. Being below 50%, section 379(2) is not attracted, though Chapter XXII still applies in full under section 379(1).
That adds the ₹6,00,000 held by non-citizen persons of Indian origin. Section 379(2) speaks of CITIZENS of India; origin, ancestry or overseas-citizen status is not the test.
There is no combination of the qualifying holders that produces this figure. It is the sort of number obtained by mixing the equity-only base with the aggregated numerator.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 379(1) · Sections applying to all foreign companies
questions.stem: Section 379(1) provides that certain sections shall apply to all foreign companies. Those sections are:

readLink.label: Read: Indian-held foreign companies — s. 379 →

options.text: Sections 380 to 386 (both inclusive) and sections 392 and 393
options.explanation: Correct. Section 379(1) applies the registration, accounts, display, service, other-provisions, fee and interpretation sections, together with the punishment and validity-of-contracts sections, to all foreign companies.

options.text: Sections 380 to 393A (both inclusive), without exception
options.explanation: Sections 387 to 391 are not confined to foreign companies at all — they bite on any person issuing a prospectus in India for a company incorporated outside India, whether or not it has a place of business here.

options.text: The whole of the Companies Act 2013, as it applies to a company incorporated in India
options.explanation: That is the consequence of section 379(2) for a substantially Indian-held foreign company, and even then only 'as if' and only for its Indian business. It is not the effect of section 379(1).

options.text: Sections 380 to 384 only, the remaining sections applying only to listed foreign companies
options.explanation: There is no listed/unlisted distinction in section 379(1), and the list runs to section 386 and then picks up sections 392 and 393.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 379(2) · Qualifying holders
questions.stem: For the purpose of the fifty per cent test in section 379(2), which of the following holdings is NOT counted?

readLink.label: Read: Indian-held foreign companies — s. 379 →

options.text: Equity shares held by a single citizen of India
options.explanation: Counted. Section 379(2) refers to 'one or more citizens of India', singly or in the aggregate.

options.text: Preference shares held by a company incorporated in India
options.explanation: Counted. The sub-section covers capital 'whether equity or preference or partly equity and partly preference', and a company incorporated in India is a qualifying holder.

options.text: Equity shares held by a body corporate incorporated in India that is not a company
options.explanation: Counted. The words are 'one or more companies or bodies corporate incorporated in India', which is wider than 'companies'.

options.text: Equity shares held by a company incorporated in Mauritius whose entire share capital is owned by Indian citizens
options.explanation: Correct. This holding is NOT counted: the test looks at bodies corporate INCORPORATED IN INDIA. A Mauritius company is not one, however Indian its ultimate ownership; the sub-section does not look through to beneficial ownership.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 379(2) · Consequence
questions.stem: Where the section 379(2) threshold is crossed, the consequence for the foreign company is that it:

readLink.label: Read: Indian-held foreign companies — s. 379 →

options.text: Is deemed to be a company incorporated in India for all purposes of the Act
options.explanation: The sub-section says 'as if it were a company incorporated in India' — a measure of compliance, not a change of legal identity. The company remains incorporated abroad and remains a foreign company under s. 2(42).

options.text: Must comply with the provisions of Chapter XXII and such other provisions of the Act as may be prescribed, with regard to the business carried on by it in India, as if it were a company incorporated in India
options.explanation: Correct. That is section 379(2) in substance — Chapter XXII plus such other provisions as are PRESCRIBED, confined to the business carried on in India, and applied on an 'as if' basis.

options.text: Must be registered afresh under section 7 within thirty days
options.explanation: There is no re-incorporation requirement anywhere in Chapter XXII. Section 7 governs the incorporation of Indian companies and has nothing to do with this.

options.text: Is exempt from the filing requirements of section 380, those being replaced by Indian-company filings
options.explanation: Section 379(2) ADDS to Chapter XXII; it does not displace it. The FC-1, FC-3 and FC-4 obligations continue to apply in full.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 379(2) · Base of the test
questions.stem: The fifty per cent threshold in section 379(2) is measured against:

readLink.label: Read: Indian-held foreign companies — s. 379 →

options.text: The voting power exercisable at a general meeting of the foreign company
options.explanation: Voting power is the test in some other provisions of the Act, but not here. Section 379(2) fixes on paid-up SHARE CAPITAL.

options.text: The turnover derived by the foreign company from its Indian business operations
options.explanation: Turnover is irrelevant to section 379(2). It has no financial-size trigger of any kind.

options.text: The paid-up share capital, whether equity or preference or partly equity and partly preference
options.explanation: Correct. The sub-section expressly covers both classes and any mixture of them, and the threshold is 'not less than fifty per cent' — so exactly half suffices.

options.text: The paid-up equity share capital only, preference capital being excluded
options.explanation: This is the standard misreading. Preference capital is expressly included, and excluding it changes both the numerator and the denominator.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 380(2) · The trigger event
questions.stem: The thirty-day period within which a foreign company must deliver the documents specified in section 380(1) to the Registrar runs from:

readLink.label: Read: Documents on establishing a place of business — s. 380 →

options.text: The date of establishment of its place of business in India
options.explanation: Correct. Section 380(2) requires delivery within thirty days of the establishment of the place of business in India — not from any earlier or later event.

options.text: The date of its incorporation in the country of origin
options.explanation: Incorporation abroad may have happened decades earlier. Chapter XXII engages only when a place of business is established in India.

options.text: The date on which it first raises an invoice on an Indian customer
options.explanation: Invoicing is evidence of business activity, but the clock is tied to the establishment of the place of business, which usually precedes the first invoice.

options.text: The close of the financial year in which the place of business was established
options.explanation: That is the trigger for the accounts and annual-return clocks under section 381 and the Rules, not for the section 380 filing.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 380(2) · FC-1 due date
questions.stem: Helios Cloudworks Pte Ltd, incorporated in Singapore, takes possession of its Bengaluru premises and begins operations on 9 March 2026. The last date for delivering the documents specified in section 380(1) to the Registrar is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 380(2) — thirty days from establishment

readLink.label: Read: Documents on establishing a place of business — s. 380 →

options.text: 24 March 2026
options.explanation: That is fifteen days. No fifteen-day period appears anywhere in Chapter XXII.

options.text: 8 April 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days counted from 9 March 2026, excluding the trigger day: March supplies 22 further days, leaving 8 days into April.

options.text: 9 April 2026
options.explanation: That reads 'thirty days' as 'one calendar month'. The section is expressed in days, and in a 31-day month the two never coincide.
That is sixty days. Sixty days is the annual-return period in the Rules, measured from the last day of the financial year — a different clock off a different event.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 380(2) · FC-1 due date
questions.stem: Belvoir Trading Ltd establishes a branch office in Kolkata on 20 January 2027. The last date for delivery of the section 380(1) documents to the Registrar is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 380(2) — thirty days from establishment

readLink.label: Read: Documents on establishing a place of business — s. 380 →

options.text: 19 February 2027
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days from 20 January 2027: January supplies 11 further days, leaving 19 days into February.

options.text: 20 February 2027
options.explanation: That is one calendar month. Section 380(2) is expressed in days.

options.text: 4 February 2027
options.explanation: That is fifteen days, a period that appears nowhere in Chapter XXII.

options.text: 21 March 2027
options.explanation: That is sixty days — the annual-return period, and one that runs from the financial-year end, not from the establishment of the place of business.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 380(1) · The document list
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT among the documents and particulars a foreign company must deliver to the Registrar under section 380(1)?

readLink.label: Read: Documents on establishing a place of business — s. 380 →

options.text: A certified copy of the charter, statutes or memorandum and articles of the company, with a certified English translation if it is not in English
options.explanation: Required by section 380(1)(a). 'Certified' is itself defined in section 386(a) as certified in the prescribed manner to be a true copy or correct translation.

options.text: Particulars of the opening and closing of a place of business in India on any earlier occasion
options.explanation: Required by section 380(1)(f). The Registrar is entitled to the company's whole Indian history, not just its current presence.

options.text: An audited balance sheet of the company for the year preceding the establishment of the place of business
options.explanation: Correct. This is NOT in the section 380(1) list. Accounts come later and separately, under section 381, and relate to the years AFTER the place of business is established.

options.text: A declaration that none of the directors of the company or the authorised representative in India has ever been convicted or debarred from formation of companies and management in India or abroad
options.explanation: Required by section 380(1)(g). Note that 'director' here carries the wider section 386(b) meaning.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · ss. 380(1)(a) and 386(a) · Certified translation
questions.stem: A foreign company's constitutional documents are in Japanese. Under Chapter XXII:

readLink.label: Read: Documents on establishing a place of business — s. 380 →

options.text: The documents need not be filed at all, the Registrar being unable to read them
options.explanation: The obligation in section 380(1)(a) is absolute. The answer to a foreign-language instrument is a translation, not an exemption.

options.text: An English translation prepared by any officer of the company is sufficient
options.explanation: The translation must be CERTIFIED, and section 386(a) defines 'certified' as certified IN THE PRESCRIBED MANNER to be a true copy or a correct translation — a rules-level formality, not the company's own say-so.

options.text: Only a summary in English of the principal clauses need be filed
options.explanation: Nothing in section 380 permits a summary. The requirement is a certified copy of the instrument, with a certified translation.

options.text: A certified translation in English must accompany the certified copy of the instrument, and the same requirement applies to the accounts filed under section 381
options.explanation: Correct. Section 380(1)(a) requires a certified English translation of a non-English instrument, and section 381(3) imposes the same requirement on any document filed with the accounts that is not in English.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · ss. 380(1)(d) and 383 · The authorised person
questions.stem: Section 380(1)(d) requires a foreign company to deliver the name and address of one or more persons resident in India authorised to accept service of process. The importance of this requirement is that:

readLink.label: Read: Display, service and fees — ss. 382, 383 and 385 →

options.text: Under section 383, service addressed to that person and left at, or sent by post or electronic mode to, that address is deemed sufficient service on the company
options.explanation: Correct. Sections 380(1)(d) and 383 are a pair: the first makes the company nominate a reachable person, the second makes service on him good service on the company.

options.text: That person becomes personally liable for all the debts of the foreign company incurred in India
options.explanation: No such liability is created. The person is an address for service, not a guarantor; he may of course be an 'officer in default' for section 392 if he is one.

options.text: That person is deemed to be a director of the foreign company for all purposes of the Act
options.explanation: The section 386(b) extension of 'director' turns on whether the Board is accustomed to act on a person's instructions, not on whether he has been named as an agent for service.

options.text: Service on the company at its registered office abroad becomes invalid
options.explanation: Section 383 provides a deemed-sufficient mode of service; it does not invalidate other modes otherwise available in law.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 380(3) · Alteration return
questions.stem: On 6 November 2026 Helios Cloudworks Pte Ltd replaces the person resident in India authorised to accept service of process on its behalf. The last date for delivering a return of the alteration to the Registrar is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 380(3) — thirty days from the alteration

readLink.label: Read: Documents on establishing a place of business — s. 380 →

options.text: 21 November 2026
options.explanation: That is fifteen days. Section 380(3) allows thirty.

options.text: 5 January 2027
options.explanation: That is sixty days — the annual-return period under the Rules, measured from the last day of the financial year.
That is six calendar months — the accounts-filing window under the Rules, again measured from the close of the financial year.

options.text: 6 December 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days from 6 November 2026: November supplies 24 further days, leaving 6 days into December. The clock runs from the date of the alteration itself.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 380(1)(g) · Declaration of no debarment
questions.stem: The declaration required by section 380(1)(g) must state that no conviction or debarment attaches to:

readLink.label: Read: Documents on establishing a place of business — s. 380 →

options.text: The subscribers to the company's charter, at the time of its incorporation abroad
options.explanation: The declaration concerns the persons who will run and represent the Indian presence, not the historical subscribers to a foreign charter.

options.text: Any of the directors of the company or the authorised representative in India, in respect of formation of companies and management, in India or abroad
options.explanation: Correct. Section 380(1)(g) covers both the directors and the authorised representative, and it is expressly not limited to Indian convictions or debarments — 'in India or abroad'.

options.text: The directors of the company only, and only in respect of offences committed in India
options.explanation: Two errors. The authorised representative in India is expressly included, and the declaration extends to conduct abroad.

options.text: Every shareholder holding more than five per cent of the paid-up capital of the company
options.explanation: Shareholders are not mentioned in section 380(1)(g) at all. The only place shareholding matters in this Chapter is the fifty per cent test in section 379(2).

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 391(1) · Misstatements in a prospectus
questions.stem: Section 391(1) applies sections 34 to 36 of the Act to:

readLink.label: Read: Misstatements, closure and punishment — ss. 391 and 392 →

options.text: Every document filed by a foreign company with the Registrar under sections 380 and 381
options.explanation: Sections 34 to 36 are the prospectus-misstatement provisions. Defective filings under sections 380 and 381 are dealt with by section 392.

options.text: The issue of shares by an Indian subsidiary of a foreign company
options.explanation: An Indian subsidiary is an Indian company and is governed by sections 34 to 36 directly; it needs no bridge through section 391.

options.text: The issue of a prospectus by a company incorporated outside India under section 389, and the issue of Indian Depository Receipts by a foreign company
options.explanation: Correct. Section 391(1) names exactly those two situations, importing criminal liability for misstatements (s. 34), civil liability for misstatements (s. 35) and punishment for fraudulently inducing persons to invest money (s. 36).

options.text: Any advertisement issued in India by a foreign company, whether or not it offers securities
options.explanation: Sections 34 to 36 attach to a PROSPECTUS and to IDRs. Ordinary advertising that offers no securities is outside them.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 381 + Rules · FC-3 filing date
questions.stem: Aurelia Systems Inc closes the financial year of its Indian business operations on 31 March 2027. Ignoring any extension the Registrar may grant, the last date for filing its financial statements with the Registrar is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 381 read with the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules 2014 — six months from the close of the financial year

readLink.label: Read: Accounts, audit and the annual return — s. 381 →

options.explanation: That is sixty days, which is the ANNUAL RETURN period. The accounts run on a six-month clock off the same year-end — the two are constantly swapped.

options.text: 30 September 2027
options.explanation: Correct. Six calendar months from the close of the financial year on 31 March 2027; September has thirty days, so the period ends on 30 September 2027. The Registrar may, for special reasons and on application, extend this by up to three further months.

options.text: 27 September 2027
options.explanation: That is 180 days counted day by day. The Rules express the accounts window in MONTHS, so the calendar-month count applies.

options.text: 31 December 2027
options.explanation: That is nine months — the outer limit only IF the Registrar has actually granted the three-month extension for special reasons. It is not the period available as of right.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 381 + Rule 4 · Audit
questions.stem: The accounts of the Indian business operations of a foreign company must be audited by:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 381 read with Rule 4, Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules 2014

readLink.label: Read: Accounts, audit and the annual return — s. 381 →

options.text: A practising chartered accountant in India, or a firm or limited liability partnership of practising chartered accountants
options.explanation: Correct. The Rules made under section 381 require the accounts of the Indian business operations to be audited by a practising chartered accountant in India, or by a firm or LLP of practising chartered accountants. The requirement is rules-level, so verify it for your attempt.

options.text: The auditor appointed by the company in its country of incorporation, whose report is accepted without more
options.explanation: The foreign auditor's report on the company as a whole does not discharge the Indian requirement. The INDIAN BUSINESS OPERATIONS must be audited here.

options.text: An auditor appointed by the members under section 139 at an annual general meeting
options.explanation: Section 139 is not among the provisions imported by section 384, and a foreign company holds no annual general meeting in India. The auditor requirement comes through the Rules, not through section 139.

options.text: The Comptroller and Auditor-General of India
options.explanation: The CAG audits government companies under section 139(5) and (7). A foreign company is not a government company merely by carrying on business here.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 381(4) · List of places of business
questions.stem: Along with the documents required by section 381(1), a foreign company must send to the Registrar:

readLink.label: Read: Accounts, audit and the annual return — s. 381 →

options.text: A list of every shareholder holding more than one per cent of its paid-up capital
options.explanation: No such list is required by section 381. Shareholding is relevant only to the separate section 379(2) computation.

options.text: A list of all its places of business anywhere in the world as at the date of the balance sheet
options.explanation: The obligation is confined to places of business established IN INDIA. Its overseas establishments are no concern of the Indian Registrar.

options.text: A list of the directors who attended the meeting at which the balance sheet was approved
options.explanation: Section 381(4) says nothing about board attendance. That is a section 128/134 style requirement for Indian companies.

options.text: A list, in the prescribed form, of all the places of business established by the company in India as at the date of the balance sheet
options.explanation: Correct. Section 381(4) requires this list to accompany the financial statements, which is why the accounts filing doubles as a running record of the company's Indian footprint.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 384(2) + Rules · FC-4 annual return
questions.stem: Aurelia Systems Inc closes its financial year on 31 March 2027. The last date for filing its annual return with the Registrar is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 384(2) read with the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules 2014 — sixty days from the last day of the financial year

readLink.label: Read: Accounts, audit and the annual return — s. 381 →

options.text: 30 April 2027
options.explanation: That is thirty days — the section 380 period, which runs from the establishment of a place of business or from an alteration, not from a year-end.
That reads sixty days as two calendar months. The Rules say days, and sixty days from 31 March lands on 30 May, not 31 May.
Correct. Sixty days counted from the last day of the financial year, 31 March 2027: April supplies thirty days and May the remaining thirty, giving 30 May 2027.

options.text: 30 September 2027
options.explanation: That is six months, which is the FINANCIAL STATEMENTS window. The annual return is the shorter of the two clocks because it does not wait on an audit.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 384(2) + Rules · FC-4 annual return
questions.stem: Kestrel Analytics Inc, a foreign company, adopts a financial year ending on 31 December. For the year ended 31 December 2026, the last date for filing its annual return is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 384(2) read with the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules 2014 — sixty days from the last day of the financial year

readLink.label: Read: Accounts, audit and the annual return — s. 381 →

options.text: 30 January 2027
options.explanation: That is thirty days. The annual-return period is sixty days from the last day of the financial year.

options.text: 1 March 2027
options.explanation: Correct. Sixty days from 31 December 2026: January supplies 31 days and February 2027 supplies 28, taking the count to 59 on 28 February, so the sixtieth day is 1 March 2027.

options.text: 28 February 2027
options.explanation: That is two calendar months, and it is also the fifty-ninth day. 2027 is not a leap year, which is exactly why the day-count and the month-count part company here.

options.text: 30 June 2027
options.explanation: That is six months — the financial-statements window, not the annual-return window.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 382(a) · Display outside the place of business
questions.stem: Section 382(a) requires a foreign company to exhibit conspicuously on the outside of every office or place where it carries on business in India:

readLink.label: Read: Display, service and fees — ss. 382, 383 and 385 →

options.text: The name of the company and the country in which it is incorporated, in legible English characters and also in the characters of a language in general use in that locality
options.explanation: Correct. Both the name AND the country of incorporation must appear, and outside the premises the display must be in English characters and in the local language.

options.text: The name of the company and the address of its registered office abroad, in English characters only
options.explanation: Two errors. The section requires the COUNTRY of incorporation, not the overseas address, and the outside display must also be in a language in general use in the locality.

options.text: The name of the company and its Corporate Identity Number
options.explanation: A CIN is allotted under section 7(3) to a company incorporated in India. A foreign company has no CIN; the section 12(3) display code for Indian companies is being confused with section 382.

options.text: The name of the company alone, the country of incorporation being required only on business letters
options.explanation: The country of incorporation is required in both places — on the signboard under clause (a) and on business letters and official publications under clause (b).

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 382(c) · Notice of limited liability
questions.stem: Where the liability of the members of a foreign company is limited, section 382(c) requires notice of that fact to be:

readLink.label: Read: Display, service and fees — ss. 382, 383 and 385 →

options.text: Filed with the Registrar in the return of alterations under section 380(3)
options.explanation: Section 380(3) deals with alterations in the section 380(1) particulars. Section 382(c) is a display and publication requirement, not a filing requirement.

options.text: Stated in the prospectus only, and nowhere else
options.explanation: The prospectus is only the first item in the clause. The notice must also appear on business letters, bill-heads, letter paper, notices, advertisements and other official publications.

options.text: Recorded in the register of members maintained at the principal place of business in India
options.explanation: Section 382(c) creates no register. It is directed at people dealing with the company, who must be able to see the limitation of liability for themselves.

options.text: Stated in every prospectus and in all business letters, bill-heads, letter paper, notices, advertisements and other official publications, and exhibited conspicuously outside every office or place of business in India, in English characters and in the local language
options.explanation: Correct. Clause (c) requires both publication and outside display, and for the outside display it repeats the English-plus-local-language requirement of clause (a).

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 383 · Service on a foreign company
questions.stem: Under section 383, a document required to be served on a foreign company is deemed sufficiently served if it is:

readLink.label: Read: Display, service and fees — ss. 382, 383 and 385 →

options.text: Sent by registered post to the company's registered office in its country of incorporation
options.explanation: That may be effective under other law, but it is not the deemed-sufficient mode section 383 provides. The section works off the Indian address filed under section 380.

options.text: Delivered to any employee of the company found at any of its Indian offices
options.explanation: Section 383 fixes on the person whose name and address were delivered to the Registrar, not on whoever happens to be present at the premises.

options.text: Addressed to any person whose name and address have been delivered to the Registrar under section 380, and left at or sent by post to that address, or sent by electronic mode
options.explanation: Correct. Section 383 makes service on the nominated resident person at the notified address good service on the company, and expressly allows electronic mode.

options.text: Published in two newspapers circulating in the locality of the principal place of business in India
options.explanation: Newspaper publication is a mode used elsewhere in the Act (for example in section 13(8)). It is not a mode of service under section 383.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 385 · Fee for registration of documents
questions.stem: Section 385 of the Companies Act 2013 provides that:

readLink.label: Read: Display, service and fees — ss. 382, 383 and 385 →

options.text: No fee is payable by a foreign company for registration of documents under this Chapter
options.explanation: The section exists precisely to impose a fee. Registration under Chapter XXII is not free.

options.text: There shall be paid to the Registrar, for registering any document required by this Chapter to be registered by him, such fee as may be prescribed
options.explanation: Correct. Section 385 is a short enabling provision; the amount of the fee is rules-level and no figure from it is examinable.

options.text: The fee payable is fixed by the section at a percentage of the foreign company's paid-up share capital
options.explanation: Section 385 fixes no amount and no formula. It simply says 'such fee as may be prescribed'.

options.text: The fee is payable to the Central Government and not to the Registrar
options.explanation: The section names the Registrar as the payee, which fits the rest of the Chapter — the Registrar is the office with which every Chapter XXII document is filed.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 384(4) · Registration of charges
questions.stem: Meridian Cloudworks Pte Ltd, a foreign company with a Pune office, mortgages (i) its Pune office building and (ii) its factory in Singapore, both to the same bank. As to registration of charges under Chapter VI:

readLink.label: Read: Which other provisions apply — s. 384 →

options.text: The charge on the Pune building must be registered, Chapter VI applying mutatis mutandis to charges on property created or acquired by a foreign company in India; the Singapore charge need not
options.explanation: Correct. Section 384(4) applies Chapter VI mutatis mutandis to charges on properties which are created or acquired by any foreign company IN INDIA. The location of the property is the test.

options.text: Both charges must be registered with the Registrar, because the chargor is a foreign company registered under section 380
options.explanation: Registration under section 380 does not extend the Indian charge regime to property outside India. Section 384(4) is expressly territorial.

options.text: Neither charge need be registered, Chapter VI applying only to companies incorporated in India
options.explanation: Section 384(4) exists to displace exactly that assumption; it applies Chapter VI to foreign companies for their Indian property.

options.text: Only the Singapore charge need be registered, because the Pune building is already disclosed under section 381(4)
options.explanation: The section 381(4) list of places of business is a disclosure of premises, not a registration of security, and it has no bearing on Chapter VI.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 384(3) · Books of account
questions.stem: Section 384(3) applies section 128 (books of account) to a foreign company:

readLink.label: Read: Which other provisions apply — s. 384 →

options.text: In respect of its worldwide operations, so that its global books must be maintained in the form section 128 requires
options.explanation: The sub-section is expressly confined to the business carried on by the foreign company in India. Its global books remain governed by the law of its own country.

options.text: Only if not less than fifty per cent of its paid-up capital is Indian-held
options.explanation: That condition belongs to section 379(2). Section 384(3) applies to every foreign company, whatever its ownership.

options.text: Only if it has issued a prospectus or Indian Depository Receipts in India
options.explanation: That kind of condition once appeared in section 391(2) before its substitution; it has never been a condition of section 384(3).

options.text: With respect to the business carried on by it in India, as those provisions apply to a company incorporated in India
options.explanation: Correct. Section 384(3) imports section 128 for the Indian business only — the same territorial limit that governs section 384(4) for charges.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 384 · What is not imported
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT applied to a foreign company by section 384?

readLink.label: Read: Which other provisions apply — s. 384 →

options.text: Section 71, relating to debentures
options.explanation: Applied by section 384(1), mutatis mutandis.

options.text: Section 92, relating to the annual return
options.explanation: Applied by section 384(2), subject to such exceptions, modifications and adaptations as may be prescribed — the enabling power behind the sixty-day annual-return filing.

options.text: Section 96, relating to the annual general meeting
options.explanation: Correct. Section 96 is NOT among the provisions section 384 imports. The section brings in only section 71, section 92, section 128, Chapter VI and Chapter XIV; the general-meeting, board-composition, auditor-appointment and dividend provisions stay out.

options.text: Chapter XIV, relating to inspection, inquiry and investigation
options.explanation: Applied by section 384(5), mutatis mutandis, so the investigative machinery of sections 206 to 229 reaches a foreign company.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 386(b) · Meaning of director
questions.stem: For the purposes of Chapter XXII, 'director' in relation to a foreign company:

readLink.label: Read: Interpretation — s. 386 →

options.text: Means only a person formally appointed to the Board under the law of the country of incorporation
options.explanation: Section 386(b) is inclusive and deliberately wider than that, precisely because a foreign board may be controlled from outside it.

options.text: Includes any person in accordance with whose directions or instructions the Board of Directors of the company is accustomed to act
options.explanation: Correct. Section 386(b) extends 'director' to the person the Board is accustomed to obey, so his particulars belong in the section 380(1) list and the section 380(1)(g) declaration covers him.

options.text: Includes every employee of the company posted to its Indian place of business
options.explanation: Posting to India is irrelevant. The test is control over the Board's decisions.

options.text: Means the person resident in India authorised under section 380(1)(d) to accept service of process
options.explanation: The authorised representative is an address for service. He is named separately in section 380(1)(d) and in the section 380(1)(g) declaration, which shows the Act treats him as distinct from the directors.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 387 · Dating and particulars of a prospectus
questions.stem: Which of the following particulars is NOT required by section 387 to be stated in a prospectus issued in India offering securities of a company incorporated outside India?

readLink.label: Read: Prospectus and IDRs — ss. 387 to 390 →

options.text: The names, addresses and shareholdings of every member of the company holding more than two per cent of its capital
options.explanation: Correct. No such particular is required by section 387. The section calls for the constitution, the incorporating enactments, an Indian address for inspection, the date and country of incorporation, and whether a place of business has been established in India.

options.text: The instrument constituting or defining the constitution of the company
options.explanation: Required by section 387(1)(a), together with the enactments under which the company was incorporated.

options.text: An address in India where the said instrument or enactments, or copies of them, can be inspected
options.explanation: Required by section 387(1)(c), with a certified translation where the instrument is not in English — the point being that an Indian investor must be able to read the constitution here.

options.text: The date on which and the country in which the company was incorporated, and whether it has established a place of business in India
options.explanation: Required by section 387(1)(d) and (e); where a place of business has been established, the address of the principal office in India must also be given.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 388 · Expert's consent
questions.stem: Section 388 provides that no person shall issue in India a prospectus of a company incorporated outside India containing a statement purporting to be made by an expert unless:

readLink.label: Read: Prospectus and IDRs — ss. 387 to 390 →

options.text: The expert is a resident of India and is registered with the Registrar
options.explanation: Section 388 imposes no residence or registration requirement on the expert. It regulates consent, not nationality.

options.text: The expert's oral consent is recorded in the minutes of the managing body
options.explanation: The consent must be IN WRITING, and a statement that it has been given and not withdrawn must appear in the prospectus itself.

options.text: The expert's consent is obtained within thirty days after the issue of the prospectus
options.explanation: Consent after the event is worthless. The consent must exist, and must not have been withdrawn, BEFORE the prospectus is issued.

options.text: The expert has given, and has not withdrawn, his written consent to the issue of the prospectus with the statement in the form and context in which it appears, and a statement to that effect appears in the prospectus
options.explanation: Correct. Section 388 requires written consent, not withdrawn, to the statement in the form and context in which it appears, plus a statement in the prospectus that the consent has been given; and the prospectus must state on its face that a copy has been delivered for registration.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 389 · Registration of the prospectus
questions.stem: Section 389 requires that, before a prospectus offering securities of a company incorporated outside India is issued, circulated or distributed in India, a copy of it must be delivered to the Registrar for registration. That copy must be certified by:

readLink.label: Read: Prospectus and IDRs — ss. 387 to 390 →

options.text: The company's Indian authorised representative alone
options.explanation: The authorised representative under section 380(1)(d) is an address for service. Section 389 requires certification at board level.

options.text: A practising chartered accountant in India
options.explanation: A practising chartered accountant audits the Indian business accounts under the Rules made under section 381. He has no certifying role under section 389.

options.text: The chairperson of the company and two other directors, as having been approved by resolution of the managing body
options.explanation: Correct. Section 389 requires a copy certified by the chairperson and two other directors as approved by resolution of the managing body, delivered for registration BEFORE issue, with expert consents and material contracts endorsed or attached, and the prospectus must state on its face that a copy has been so delivered.

options.text: The Registrar of the country in which the company is incorporated
options.explanation: No foreign official certifies an Indian prospectus. Certification is by the company's own chairperson and two directors, on the strength of a managing-body resolution.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 390 · Indian Depository Receipts
questions.stem: Section 390 of the Companies Act 2013 deals with the offer of Indian Depository Receipts. It provides that:

readLink.label: Read: Prospectus and IDRs — ss. 387 to 390 →

options.text: Only a foreign company that has already established a place of business in India may issue Indian Depository Receipts
options.explanation: The section applies to a company incorporated or to be incorporated outside India 'whether or not it has established, or will establish, any place of business in India'.

options.text: The Central Government may make rules as to the offer of Indian Depository Receipts, the disclosures required in the prospectus or letter of offer, the manner of dealing with them in a depository mode and by custodian and underwriters, and the manner of their sale, transfer or transmission
options.explanation: Correct. Section 390 is an enabling provision with those four heads; every operative condition for IDRs is rules-level and sits outside the section itself.

options.text: Indian Depository Receipts may be issued only against the debentures of a company incorporated outside India
options.explanation: Section 390 does not confine IDRs to any particular class of underlying security, and in practice IDRs are issued against the underlying equity of a foreign issuer.

options.text: Indian Depository Receipts are exempt from sections 34 to 36 relating to misstatements
options.explanation: The opposite. Section 391(1)(ii) expressly applies sections 34 to 36 to the issue of Indian Depository Receipts by a foreign company.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 393 · Validity of contracts
questions.stem: Nordwind Marine GmbH established a place of business in Kochi but has filed nothing at all under Chapter XXII. It now wishes to sue an Indian supplier on a contract made through that office. Under section 393:

readLink.label: Read: Validity of contracts and exemptions — ss. 393 and 393A →

options.text: The contract remains valid and the company remains liable to be sued on it, but the company cannot bring the suit, claim a set-off, make a counter-claim or institute any legal proceeding in respect of it until it has complied with the provisions of the Act applicable to it
options.explanation: Correct. Section 393 preserves the validity of the contract and the company's liability to be sued, while disabling the company from suing until it complies. Non-compliance takes away the sword, never the shield — and the bar lifts on compliance.

options.text: The contract is void, so neither party can sue on it
options.explanation: Section 393 says in terms that the failure 'shall not affect the validity of any contract, dealing or transaction'. Voidness is the trap answer here.

options.text: The company may sue, but any decree obtained will be unenforceable until the filings are made
options.explanation: The section bars the institution of the proceeding itself, not merely the execution of a decree.

options.text: The bar on suing is permanent, and cannot be cured by making the filings later
options.explanation: The section says 'until the company has complied'. Subsequent compliance restores the company's right to sue, which is why the practical advice is simply to file and then sue.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 2(42) · Meaning of a foreign company
questions.stem: Define a 'foreign company' under the Companies Act 2013 and explain the requirements that must be satisfied before a company incorporated outside India is treated as one. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 2(42): a 'foreign company' means any company or body corporate incorporated outside India which (a) has a place of business in India, whether by itself or through an agent, physically or through electronic mode, and (b) conducts any business activity in India in any other manner

All the limbs must be satisfied together: incorporation outside India; a place of business in India; and the conduct of business activity in India. A company that merely trades WITH India, without any place of business here, is not a foreign company; nor is one that keeps premises here but conducts no business activity

'Place of business' is not exhaustively defined; section 386(c) provides that it INCLUDES a share transfer or registration office, and the presence may be maintained by the company itself or through an agent

'Electronic mode' is defined in Rule 2(1)(c) of the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules 2014 and is very wide — business-to-business and business-to-consumer transactions, data interchange, offering or accepting deposits or subscriptions in securities in India or from citizens of India, financial settlements, web-based marketing, advisory, database and supply-chain services, and online services — and it applies whether or not the main server is installed in India (rules-level, amendment-sensitive)
skeleton.citation: Rule 2(1)(c), Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules 2014

skeleton.point: An isolated transaction concluded in India does not by itself amount to establishing a place of business; what the definition contemplates is a settled, continuing presence from which business is done
skeleton.citation: ICAI SM P2 Ch 11 — analysis of s. 2(42)

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 380 · Documents to be delivered to the Registrar
questions.stem: A company incorporated in Japan proposes to open a branch office in Chennai. State the documents and particulars it must deliver to the Registrar, the time within which it must do so, and its obligation where those particulars later change. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 380(2): the documents must be delivered to the Registrar for registration within THIRTY DAYS of the establishment of the place of business in India; the clock runs from establishment, not from incorporation abroad or from the first invoice

Section 380(1)(a) to (h): a certified copy of the charter, statutes or memorandum and articles or other instrument constituting or defining the constitution of the company, with a certified English translation if it is not in English; the full address of the registered or principal office of the company; a list of the directors and secretary with the prescribed particulars; the name and address of one or more persons resident in India authorised to accept service of process and other documents on behalf of the company; the full address of the office in India deemed to be its principal place of business; particulars of the opening and closing of a place of business in India on any earlier occasion; a declaration that none of the directors or the authorised representative in India has ever been convicted or debarred from formation of companies and management, in India or abroad; and any other prescribed information

Section 380(3): where any alteration is made or occurs in any of those particulars, the company must deliver to the Registrar, within THIRTY DAYS of the alteration, a return containing the particulars of the alteration

Practical and consequential points: the filings are made in the prescribed forms (FC-1 for the initial filing and FC-2 for alterations — rules-level) on payment of the fee prescribed under section 385; failure attracts the fine under section 392, and under section 393 the company cannot sue in India until it complies
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, ss. 385, 392 and 393; Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules 2014

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 381 · Accounts of a foreign company
questions.stem: Explain the obligations of a foreign company in relation to its accounts under section 381 of the Companies Act 2013, and state the time limits within which its financial statements and its annual return must be filed. (4 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 381(1) and (2): every foreign company shall, in every calendar year, make out a balance sheet and profit and loss account in the prescribed form, containing the prescribed particulars and including or having annexed the prescribed documents, and deliver a copy to the Registrar, together with the prescribed documents relating to its latest consolidated financial statements

Section 381(3) and (4): where any document is not in English, a certified translation must be annexed; and the company must send with those documents a list, in the prescribed form, of all the places of business established by it in India as at the date of the balance sheet

Rules-level requirements: the statements are prepared, as far as may be, in respect of the Indian business operations in accordance with Schedule III as applicable, and the accounts of the Indian business operations must be audited by a practising chartered accountant in India or by a firm or LLP of practising chartered accountants
skeleton.citation: Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules 2014, Rule 4

skeleton.point: Time limits: the financial statements, with the list of places of business, are filed within SIX MONTHS of the close of the financial year (extendable by the Registrar by up to three months, for special reasons, on application); the annual return is filed within SIXTY DAYS from the last day of the financial year under section 384(2) and the Rules — both clocks run from the same year-end and must not be interchanged
skeleton.citation: Companies Act 2013, s. 384(2) read with the Companies (Registration of Foreign Companies) Rules 2014

questions.topic: Ch 11 · s. 379(2) · Substantially Indian-held foreign companies
questions.stem: Zenith Holdings Ltd is incorporated in Mauritius and has a branch office in Ahmedabad. Its paid-up share capital consists of ₹30,00,000 of equity and ₹10,00,000 of preference. Indian citizens hold ₹11,00,000 of the equity, a company incorporated in India holds ₹6,00,000 of the equity and ₹3,00,000 of the preference, and the balance is held by non-residents who are not citizens of India. Examine whether section 379(2) of the Companies Act 2013 applies, and state its effect. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: State the provision: where not less than fifty per cent of the paid-up share capital — whether equity or preference or partly equity and partly preference — of a company incorporated outside India and having a place of business in India is held by one or more citizens of India, or by one or more companies or bodies corporate incorporated in India, or by any combination of them, whether singly or in the aggregate, section 379(2) is attracted

Identify the qualifying holders: only citizens of India and companies or bodies corporate INCORPORATED IN INDIA count; non-citizens are excluded however close their connection with India, and a foreign-incorporated company does not qualify even if it is wholly Indian-owned

Compute: total paid-up share capital = ₹30,00,000 + ₹10,00,000 = ₹40,00,000. Qualifying holding = ₹11,00,000 (Indian citizens) + ₹6,00,000 + ₹3,00,000 (Indian-incorporated company) = ₹20,00,000, i.e. exactly 50% of ₹40,00,000. Since the threshold is 'NOT LESS THAN fifty per cent', an exact half satisfies it, and the preference capital must be included in both the numerator and the denominator

Conclusion and effect: section 379(2) applies. Zenith Holdings Ltd must comply with the provisions of Chapter XXII and such other provisions of the Act as may be prescribed, with regard to the business carried on by it in India, as if it were a company incorporated in India

Qualify the conclusion: the company does not become an Indian company and is not required to re-incorporate under section 7; it remains a foreign company under section 2(42), the additional compliance is on an 'as if' basis and is limited to its Indian business, and the Chapter XXII obligations (sections 380 to 386, 392 and 393) continue to apply in full under section 379(1)

questions.topic: Ch 11 · ss. 382 to 385 · Display, service and the imported provisions
questions.stem: State the requirements as to display of the name of a foreign company, the manner in which documents may be served on it, and the provisions of the Companies Act 2013 that section 384 applies to it. (6 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 382(a): every foreign company shall conspicuously exhibit on the outside of every office or place where it carries on business in India the name of the company and the country in which it is incorporated, in letters easily legible in English characters and also in the characters of the language or one of the languages in general use in that locality

Section 382(b) and (c): the name of the company and the country of incorporation must be stated in legible English characters in all business letters, bill-heads and letter paper and in all notices and other official publications; and, where the liability of the members is limited, notice of that fact must be stated in every prospectus and in all business letters, bill-heads, letter paper, notices, advertisements and other official publications, and exhibited conspicuously outside every office or place of business in English characters and in the local language

Section 383: any process, notice or other document required to be served on a foreign company is deemed sufficiently served if addressed to any person whose name and address have been delivered to the Registrar under section 380 and left at, or sent by post to, that address, or sent by electronic mode — the provision working in tandem with section 380(1)(d)

Section 384 mapping: sub-section (1) applies section 71 (debentures) mutatis mutandis; sub-section (2) applies section 92 (annual return) subject to such exceptions, modifications and adaptations as may be prescribed; sub-section (3) applies section 128 (books of account) with respect to the business carried on in India; sub-section (4) applies Chapter VI (registration of charges) mutatis mutandis to charges on properties created or acquired by the foreign company in India; sub-section (5) applies Chapter XIV (inspection, inquiry and investigation) mutatis mutandis

Two limits worth stating: sections 384(3) and 384(4) are territorial — they reach the Indian business and property situated in India only; and section 384 imports nothing beyond the five heads named, so the annual-general-meeting, board-composition, section 139 auditor-appointment and dividend provisions do not apply to a foreign company as such
Section 385: there shall be paid to the Registrar, for registering any document required by Chapter XXII to be registered by him, such fee as may be prescribed

questions.topic: Ch 11 · ss. 391 to 393A · Consequences of non-compliance
questions.stem: A foreign company carrying on business in India through a place of business established two years ago has made no filing under Chapter XXII of the Companies Act 2013. Explain the consequences, and state the power of the Central Government to grant exemptions under that Chapter. (5 marks)

skeleton.point: Section 392: if a foreign company contravenes the provisions of Chapter XXII, the company is punishable with a fine of not less than ₹1,00,000 which may extend to ₹3,00,000, and in the case of a continuing offence with an additional fine which may extend to ₹50,000 for every day after the first during which the contravention continues (amendment-sensitive figures)

Section 392, officer liability: every officer of the foreign company who is in default is punishable with a fine of not less than ₹25,000 which may extend to ₹5,00,000; for this purpose 'director' bears the wider meaning in section 386(b) and includes a person in accordance with whose directions or instructions the Board is accustomed to act

Section 393: the failure does NOT affect the validity of any contract, dealing or transaction entered into by the company, or its liability to be sued in respect thereof; but the company shall not be entitled to bring any suit, claim any set-off, make any counter-claim or institute any legal proceeding in respect of any such contract, dealing or transaction until it has complied with the provisions of the Act applicable to it

Section 391: sections 34 to 36 (criminal liability for misstatements in a prospectus, civil liability for misstatements, and punishment for fraudulently inducing persons to invest money) apply to a prospectus issued by a company incorporated outside India under section 389 and to the issue of Indian Depository Receipts by a foreign company; and Chapter XX (winding up) applies mutatis mutandis for the closure of the place of business of a foreign company in India as if it were a company incorporated in India

Section 393A: the Central Government may, by notification, exempt any class or classes of foreign companies from any of the provisions of sections 380 to 386 and sections 392 and 393; a copy of every such notification must, as soon as may be after it is made, be laid before both Houses of Parliament. The power does not extend to section 379 or to sections 387 to 391

questions.topic: Ch 11 · Case: a Singapore company opens a Pune branch
questions.case: Meridian Cloudworks Pte Ltd is incorporated in Singapore. On 14 May 2026 it takes possession of a branch office in Pune, staffs it with sixty engineers and begins providing services to Indian customers from those premises. Its paid-up share capital is ₹60,00,000, made up of ₹52,00,000 of equity and ₹8,00,000 of preference. Of the equity, ₹14,00,000 is held by citizens of India and ₹22,00,000 by Sundar Infotech Private Limited, a company incorporated in India, the balance being held by its Singapore parent. Of the preference, ₹3,00,000 is held by Sundar Infotech Private Limited and the balance by the Singapore parent. The company has appointed Ms Anagha Rao, resident in Pune, to accept service of process on its behalf.

readLink.label: Read: Documents on establishing a place of business — s. 380 →

questions.stem: The last date by which Meridian Cloudworks Pte Ltd must deliver the documents specified in section 380(1) to the Registrar is:
questions.sourceRef: Companies Act 2013, s. 380(2) — thirty days from establishment

options.explanation: That is fifteen days. Chapter XXII contains no fifteen-day period.

options.text: 14 June 2026
options.explanation: That reads thirty days as one calendar month. May has 31 days, so the two diverge by a day.

options.text: 13 June 2026
options.explanation: Correct. Thirty days from 14 May 2026: May supplies 17 further days, leaving 13 days into June.

options.text: 13 July 2026
options.explanation: That is sixty days — the annual-return period, which runs from the last day of the financial year and not from the establishment of the place of business.

questions.stem: Meridian Cloudworks Pte Ltd is a foreign company because:

options.text: It is incorporated outside India, it has a place of business in India, and it conducts business activity in India — all three limbs of section 2(42) being satisfied
options.explanation: Correct. Incorporation in Singapore, the Pune branch and the provision of services to Indian customers from those premises satisfy the three cumulative limbs of section 2(42).

options.text: More than fifty per cent of its paid-up capital is held by Indian citizens and an Indian company
options.explanation: Indian shareholding is the trigger for the ADDITIONAL obligation in section 379(2). It plays no part in the section 2(42) definition, which would be satisfied even if the company were wholly foreign-owned.

options.text: It has appointed a person resident in India to accept service of process
options.explanation: That appointment is a CONSEQUENCE of being a foreign company — section 380(1)(d) requires it. It cannot also be the reason the company is one.

options.text: Its services are supplied to customers located in India
options.explanation: Supplying customers in India, without any place of business here, would leave the second limb unsatisfied. It is the Pune branch that makes the difference.

questions.stem: The percentage of the paid-up share capital of Meridian Cloudworks Pte Ltd held by citizens of India and by bodies corporate incorporated in India, for the purposes of section 379(2), is:

options.explanation: That counts only the equity held by the qualifying holders (₹14,00,000 + ₹22,00,000 = ₹36,00,000) against total capital of ₹60,00,000, dropping the ₹3,00,000 of preference from the numerator. Section 379(2) covers equity AND preference.
That is the Indian citizens' ₹14,00,000 alone. The sub-section aggregates citizens of India and Indian-incorporated bodies corporate, singly or in the aggregate.
That is Sundar Infotech Private Limited's total holding of ₹25,00,000 alone. The Indian citizens' holding must be added to it.

Correct. Qualifying holding = ₹14,00,000 + ₹22,00,000 + ₹3,00,000 = ₹39,00,000 against total paid-up share capital of ₹60,00,000, which is 65% — comfortably above the 'not less than fifty per cent' threshold.

questions.stem: Given that computation, the consequence for Meridian Cloudworks Pte Ltd is that it:

options.text: Is relieved of the filing obligations in sections 380 and 381, Indian-company filings taking their place
options.explanation: Section 379(2) adds to Chapter XXII; it does not displace it. Sections 380 to 386 continue to apply under section 379(1).

options.text: Must comply with Chapter XXII and such other provisions of the Act as may be prescribed, with regard to the business carried on by it in India, as if it were a company incorporated in India
options.explanation: Correct. That is the effect of section 379(2) — an 'as if' standard of compliance, confined to the Indian business, layered on top of the Chapter XXII obligations that already apply.

options.text: Ceases to be a foreign company and becomes an Indian company from the date the threshold was crossed
options.explanation: The company remains incorporated in Singapore and remains a foreign company under section 2(42). Only the measure of compliance changes.

options.text: Must convert its Pune branch into a subsidiary incorporated in India within thirty days
options.explanation: No such requirement exists anywhere in Chapter XXII. Section 379(2) imposes compliance obligations, not a restructuring.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · Case: an overseas issuer raising money in India
questions.case: Aurelia Systems Inc, incorporated in Delaware, proposes to offer its shares to investors in India. A merchant banker in Mumbai prepares a prospectus that includes a valuation report by an independent valuer and circulates it to prospective investors in India on 3 August 2026. No copy of the prospectus was delivered to the Registrar before circulation, the valuer's written consent was obtained only on 20 August 2026, and the prospectus contains a materially untrue statement about the company's order book. Aurelia Systems Inc has a branch office in Hyderabad which it registered under section 380 in 2024.

readLink.label: Read: Prospectus and IDRs — ss. 387 to 390 →

questions.stem: On the delivery of the prospectus to the Registrar, the correct position under section 389 is that:

options.text: Delivery for registration was unnecessary, because the company already has a registered place of business in India
options.explanation: Section 389 applies whether or not the company has established a place of business in India. Registration under section 380 is a separate obligation and does not dispense with it.

options.text: Delivery for registration may be made within thirty days after circulation
options.explanation: There is no post-issue window. Section 389 makes registration a precondition of issue, circulation or distribution.

options.text: Delivery for registration is required only where the offer exceeds a prescribed value
options.explanation: Section 389 contains no threshold of any kind.

options.text: A copy certified by the chairperson and two other directors as approved by resolution of the managing body had to be delivered to the Registrar BEFORE the prospectus was issued, circulated or distributed, and the prospectus had to state on its face that this had been done
options.explanation: Correct. Section 389 requires prior delivery for registration of a copy so certified, with expert consents and material contracts endorsed or attached, and a statement on the face of the prospectus that a copy has been delivered. Circulating on 3 August without any such delivery contravenes the section.

questions.stem: As to the valuer's consent obtained on 20 August 2026, section 388 requires that:

options.text: The consent be obtained within thirty days of the issue of the prospectus, which was done
options.explanation: Section 388 provides no such period. Consent obtained after circulation cannot retrospectively validate the issue.

options.text: The consent be given orally and recorded in the minutes of the managing body
options.explanation: The consent must be in writing, and a statement that it has been given and not withdrawn must appear in the prospectus itself.

options.text: The expert must have given, and not withdrawn, his written consent to the issue of the prospectus with the statement in the form and context in which it appears, and a statement to that effect must appear in the prospectus — so obtaining consent on 20 August, after circulation on 3 August, does not satisfy the section
options.explanation: Correct. Consent must exist and must be subsisting before issue, and the prospectus must say so; consent obtained seventeen days later is a contravention of section 388.

options.text: Only the company's own directors, and not an independent valuer, can be treated as experts
options.explanation: An expert is a person qualified to give a report or valuation; independence is a feature of the role, and the section is not confined to directors.

questions.stem: As to the materially untrue statement about the order book, the position under section 391(1) is that:

options.text: Sections 34 to 36 apply, so every person who authorised the issue may be liable under section 447 for a misstatement, compensation is payable under section 35 to subscribers who sustain loss, and section 36 applies to fraudulent inducement to invest
options.explanation: Correct. Section 391(1) applies sections 34 to 36 to a prospectus issued by a company incorporated outside India under section 389 and to the issue of Indian Depository Receipts by a foreign company, subject to the statutory defences in those sections.

options.text: Sections 34 to 36 apply only to companies incorporated in India, and the investors' only remedy is under the general law of misrepresentation
options.explanation: That is precisely the gap section 391(1) closes; the misstatement code follows the prospectus into India.

options.text: Sections 34 to 36 apply only where the foreign company has NOT established a place of business in India
options.explanation: Section 391(1) draws no such distinction. It fixes on the issue of a section 389 prospectus or of Indian Depository Receipts.

options.text: Liability arises only if the company is subsequently wound up in India
options.explanation: Liability under sections 34 to 36 arises on the misstatement, not on any subsequent insolvency.

questions.stem: Aurelia Systems Inc asks whether the Central Government could exempt it from these requirements. The correct advice under section 393A is that the Central Government may, by notification, exempt classes of foreign companies from:

options.text: Any provision of the Companies Act 2013, on an application by the company concerned
options.explanation: Section 393A is neither that wide nor application-based. It operates by notification and in respect of classes of foreign companies, not individual applicants.

options.text: Any of the provisions of sections 380 to 386 and sections 392 and 393 — but not from section 379, and not from the prospectus and Indian Depository Receipt provisions in sections 387 to 391
options.explanation: Correct. Section 393A names sections 380 to 386 and sections 392 and 393 only, and every such notification must, as soon as may be after it is made, be laid before both Houses of Parliament.

options.text: Sections 387 to 391 only, those being the provisions that affect capital raising
options.explanation: Those are exactly the sections section 393A does NOT reach, which is why no exemption can cure the section 388 and section 389 defaults here.

options.text: Any provision of Chapter XXII, provided the Registrar consents
options.explanation: The Registrar has no role in section 393A, and the power does not extend to the whole Chapter.

questions.topic: Ch 11 · Case: annual compliance and closure
questions.case: Kestrel Analytics Inc, incorporated in the United States, has a registered place of business in Gurugram and adopts a financial year ending on 30 June.
